name: Hyperemesis gravidarum
subtitle: Early pregnancy vomiting
oneLine: Intractable early pregnancy nausea and vomiting causing dehydration, ketosis, weight loss, and metabolic derangements

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: In early pregnancy vomiting, note age, primigravida status, occupation, and home support; young nulliparous women and those lacking domestic support are at increased risk of delayed presentation and severe dehydration.

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: A typical hyperemesis presentation reads in days to weeks: persistent nausea and vomiting 10 to 15 times daily starting at 6 to 8 weeks, with complete inability to retain oral fluids for 24 to 48 hours.

skill.hx.obg.booking_lmp.expect: Establish exact gestational age by reliable LMP or ultrasound; hyperemesis peaks between 8 and 11 weeks and typically settles by 16 to 20 weeks.

skill.hx.hyperemesi.symptoms.expect: Document vomiting frequency, absence of oral fluid tolerance, percentage weight loss exceeding five percent, reduced urinary frequency with dark urine, and screen for Wernicke encephalopathy and haematemesis.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history

skill.hx.hyperemesi.risk.expect: Ask about hyperemesis in previous pregnancies (recurrence is common, with severe hyperemesis recurring in about 1 in 5 later pregnancies), family history in mother or sisters, multiple pregnancy, molar pregnancy, and stop oral iron supplements immediately.

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for visible exhaustion, sunken eyes, dry furred tongue, dry mucous membranes, loss of skin turgor, and ketotic breath odour.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Check for resting tachycardia and postural hypotension; an orthostatic drop in blood pressure with compensatory tachycardia signifies significant intravascular hypovolaemia.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Absence of peripheral oedema is standard; check for delayed capillary refill time exceeding two seconds as a sign of peripheral hypoperfusion.

skill.exam.obg.fundal_height.expect: In early pregnancy under 12 weeks, the uterus is pelvic and should not be palpable above the symphysis pubis; a fundus palpable above dates suggests multiple gestation or gestational trophoblastic disease (hydatidiform mole).

chapters.title: Putting the hyperemesis gravidarum picture together

stations.title: Acute assessment and emergency resuscitation in severe hyperemesis gravidarum
stations.task: A 24-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation presents with 7 days of intractable vomiting, unable to keep fluids down. She is orthostatic and tachycardic with 3+ ketones on urine dipstick. Formulate your immediate emergency resuscitation plan, select appropriate intravenous fluids, outline essential safety precautions, and justify your management to the examiner.
examinerQuestions: Which intravenous fluid will you infuse first, and why must glucose-containing solutions be avoided initially?
Why is parenteral thiamine administration mandatory, and what classic clinical triad signals Wernicke encephalopathy?
What electrolyte derangement is typical of prolonged vomiting, and how should it be safely replaced?
Name two obstetric conditions associated with abnormally high hCG that must be excluded by early ultrasound.

stations.title: Focused history, severity assessment, and antiemetic counselling in early pregnancy vomiting
stations.task: Take a focused 6-minute history from this pregnant woman presenting with severe vomiting in her first trimester. Quantify her symptom severity using clinical criteria and the PUQE score, enquire into red flag symptoms, explain the diagnosis, and counsel her on the stepwise antiemetic plan.
examinerQuestions: How do you distinguish hyperemesis gravidarum from common physiological morning sickness?
Explain how the PUQE score categorises severity and guides your decision for hospital admission.

What counselling will you provide regarding the risk of recurrence in a future pregnancy, given that recurrence is common and severe hyperemesis recurs in about 1 in 5?

skill.hyperemesi.basics.title: Basics of hyperemesis gravidarum
skill.hyperemesi.basics.oneLine: Definition, epidemiology, hormonal drivers, and the differentiation from physiological pregnancy sickness
skill.hyperemesi.basics.why: Hyperemesis gravidarum is not mere morning sickness; it is a clinical syndrome of intractable vomiting causing dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, ketonuria, and weight loss exceeding five percent of pre-pregnancy weight. Defining this threshold prevents undertreating severely dehydrated mothers and avoids inappropriate diagnostic delays.

teach.heading: Definition and Core Diagnostic Triad
teach.body:
Hyperemesis gravidarum affects up to three percent of pregnancies, presenting as severe, protracted nausea and vomiting in early gestation. Unlike benign pregnancy sickness, it leads to objective volume depletion, ketonuria, and electrolyte derangements.

The classic diagnostic criteria require onset in the first trimester, persistent vomiting unrelated to other causes, ketonuria on dipstick testing, and objective weight loss exceeding five percent of measured pre-pregnancy weight.

teach.heading: Hormonal and Molecular Pathophysiology
teach.body:
The exact aetiology is multifactorial. Rapidly rising concentrations of human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) and oestrogens strongly correlate with symptom severity, explaining why sickness peaks between eight and eleven weeks gestation.

Conditions with high placental volume, such as twin gestation and hydatidiform mole, produce markedly exaggerated hCG levels and higher rates of hyperemesis. Recent genomic discoveries highlight placental GDF15 acting on the maternal brainstem emetic centre.

probes.q: What objective weight loss threshold defines hyperemesis gravidarum?
probes.a: Loss of more than five percent of pre-pregnancy weight.

probes.q: Which placental hormone peaks between 8 and 11 weeks and is strongly implicated in hyperemesis?
probes.a: Human chorionic gonadotrophin or hCG.

probes.q: Which newly identified circulating peptide hormone acts on brainstem emetic circuits in hyperemesis?
probes.a: Growth differentiation factor 15 or GDF15.

rubric.text: Defines intractable vomiting, weight loss over 5 percent, and ketonuria
Identifies hCG, oestrogen, and GDF15 as biological drivers
Contrasts physiological morning sickness with pathological hyperemesis

skill.hyperemesi.signs.title: The hyperemesis gravidarum picture
skill.hyperemesi.signs.oneLine: Clinical manifestations of severe dehydration, starvation ketosis, electrolyte derangements, and neurological risks
skill.hyperemesi.signs.why: Prolonged emesis depletes fluid, hydrogen, potassium, and chloride ions, producing hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, hypokalaemia, and prerenal azotaemia. Identifying dehydration signs early and recognising the danger signs of thiamine deficiency protects against circulatory collapse, acute kidney injury, and irreversible neurological damage.

teach.heading: Volume Depletion and Physical Signs
teach.body:
Profound fluid loss manifests with sunken eyes, dry furred tongue, cracked lips, and reduced skin elasticity. Breath carries a characteristic sweetish, acetone odour from circulating acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.

Cardiovascular examination reveals resting tachycardia and orthostatic hypotension, with a systolic drop exceeding twenty millimetres of mercury on standing. Peripheral perfusion is compromised, causing cool extremities and prolonged capillary refill.

teach.heading: Acid-Base and Electrolyte Derangements
teach.body:
Gastric juice contains high concentrations of hydrochloric acid, potassium, and sodium. Protracted loss of gastric acid produces hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Renal hydrogen ion retention is overwhelmed, leading to paradoxical aciduria.

Starvation forces the body to metabolise adipose triglycerides, generating ketone bodies that spill into the urine. Severe hypokalaemia triggers skeletal muscle weakness, ileus, and cardiac rhythm disturbances.

rows: Prolonged volume depletion reducing renal perfusion
Oliguria with raised urea and creatinine

probes.q: What characteristic breath odour is detected in severe starvation ketosis?
probes.a: A sweetish, acetone odour on the breath.

probes.q: What classic metabolic and electrolyte derangement is caused by persistent gastric acid loss?
probes.a: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

probes.q: What is the classic clinical triad of Wernicke encephalopathy in hyperemesis?
probes.a: Nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion.

rubric.text: Identifies clinical signs of volume contraction, dry mucous membranes, and postural hypotension
Explains hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and starvation ketosis
Recognises nystagmus, ataxia, and confusion as signs of acute thiamine deficiency

skill.annex.hyperemesi.puqe.title: Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis (PUQE-24) score
skill.annex.hyperemesi.puqe.oneLine: Validated 24-hour scoring tool to categorise severity and guide admission and antiemetic escalation
skill.annex.hyperemesi.puqe.why: The PUQE-24 score provides an objective, reproducible metric for assessing vomiting, nausea duration, and retching over 24 hours. Using this validated score standardises triage, distinguishes outpatient candidates from those requiring day-case or inpatient admission, and monitors therapeutic response to antiemetic protocols.

teach.heading: The Three Domains of the PUQE-24 Score
teach.body:
The Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis (PUQE-24) score evaluates three core clinical domains over the previous twenty-four hours: duration of nausea, number of vomiting episodes, and frequency of dry heaves or retching.

Each domain is scored on an ordinal scale from one (no symptoms) to five (severe intractable symptoms), yielding a composite total score ranging between three and fifteen points.

teach.heading: PUQE-24 Scoring Matrix and Triage Thresholds

probes.q: What three symptom domains are scored in the PUQE-24 tool?
probes.a: Duration of nausea, number of vomiting episodes, and frequency of retching or dry heaves.

probes.q: What total score range on the PUQE-24 scale defines severe hyperemesis gravidarum?
probes.a: A score of 13 to 15 points indicates severe hyperemesis.

probes.q: What clinical management is indicated for a patient with a moderate PUQE score of 7 to 12?
probes.a: Ambulatory daycare rehydration, parental or oral antiemetics, and active monitoring.

rubric.text: States the three domains of nausea duration, vomiting episodes, and retching
Categorises mild (3-6), moderate (7-12), and severe (13-15) scoring bands
Matches score categories to outpatient, ambulatory daycare, or inpatient admission

skill.hyperemesi.summary.title: The clinical summary in hyperemesis gravidarum
skill.hyperemesi.summary.oneLine: Synthesising gestational age, vomiting severity, degree of dehydration, biochemical derangement, and risk profile
skill.hyperemesi.summary.why: A precise clinical summary crystallises the diagnosis, quantifies dehydration and weight loss, reports acid-base and electrolyte status, and confirms the exclusion of secondary causes. A clear summary ensures the clinical team prioritises immediate thiamine administration before glucose-containing infusions.

teach.heading: Core Components of the Clinical Synthesis
teach.body:
A structured summary begins with age, gravidity, parity, and ultrasound-confirmed gestational age. It states the duration and daily frequency of vomiting, and records percentage weight loss against pre-pregnancy baseline.

It documents hydration status, highlighting orthostatic vital signs, ketonuria, and electrolyte derangements including hypokalaemia. Finally, it confirms exclusion of alternative surgical, infectious, or trophoblastic conditions.

teach.heading: Standard Exemplar Clinical Summary
teach.body:
This is a 24-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks gestation with severe hyperemesis gravidarum, demonstrated by a PUQE score of 14, 6.7 percent weight loss, and 3+ ketonuria.

She has marked volume depletion with orthostatic tachycardia and hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Pelvic ultrasound confirms a viable singleton pregnancy, excluding molar disease. She requires urgent crystalloid resuscitation, thiamine before dextrose, and antiemetic escalation.

probes.q: What four core elements should every hyperemesis summary contain?
probes.a: Gestational age, severity of vomiting with weight loss, hydration and electrolyte status, and confirmation of viable intrauterine singleton pregnancy.

probes.q: Why must the clinical summary explicitly note whether ultrasound has excluded molar pregnancy?
probes.a: Because hydatidiform mole causes high hCG levels and severe vomiting, requiring evacuation rather than supportive medical management.

probes.q: What prescribing priority must be communicated in the management summary before any glucose is hung?
probes.a: Parenteral thiamine must be administered before or with dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

rubric.text: Synthesises gestational age, PUQE score, percentage weight loss, and ketonuria
Reports hypokalaemia, acid-base derangement, and ultrasound exclusion of molar gestation
Articulates crystalloid resuscitation, antiemetic escalation, and thiamine before dextrose

skill.hyperemesi.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of severe vomiting in early pregnancy
skill.hyperemesi.differential.oneLine: Distinguishing hyperemesis from gestational trophoblastic disease, twins, and gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, and endocrine disorders
skill.hyperemesi.differential.why: Attributing all vomiting in early pregnancy to hyperemesis is a dangerous pitfall that delays recognition of molar pregnancy, acute pyelonephritis, appendicitis, or diabetic ketoacidosis. Hyperemesis is a diagnosis of exclusion; evaluating fever, severe localized abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, or altered sensorium directs immediate alternative workup.

teach.heading: Obstetric Differentials: Trophoblast and Plurality
teach.body:
Conditions with high circulating hCG levels lead the obstetric differential. Gestational trophoblastic disease (hydatidiform mole) presents with exaggerated vomiting, vaginal bleeding, uterus larger than dates, and bilateral theca lutein cysts.

Multiple gestation similarly amplifies placental hormone secretion, producing severe sickness. Urgent pelvic ultrasonography differentiates these entities by demonstrating either multiple viable sacs or classic vesicular snowstorm changes.

teach.heading: Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary Mimics
teach.body:
Acute gastroenteritis is distinguished by watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramping, and sick contacts, resolving within forty-eight hours. Acute appendicitis in pregnancy produces fever, leucocytosis, and persistent right lower quadrant tenderness.

Acute pyelonephritis presents with high spiking fevers, chills, and renal angle tenderness. Peptic ulcer disease presents with burning epigastric pain and may produce haematemesis without prominent systemic ketosis.

rows: Severe epigastric pain radiating to back
Serum lipase elevated more than 3 times
Right upper quadrant pain, Murphy sign
Elevated blood glucose, high anion gap
Positive TSH receptor (TRAb) antibodies favour Graves disease

probes.q: Why is pelvic ultrasonography mandatory before confirming hyperemesis gravidarum?
probes.a: To exclude molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole) and multiple pregnancy.

probes.q: What laboratory finding differentiates diabetic ketoacidosis from starvation ketosis in hyperemesis?
probes.a: Marked hyperglycaemia and high anion gap metabolic acidosis occur in diabetic ketoacidosis, whereas hyperemesis patients are euglycaemic.

probes.q: Which serum enzyme elevation confirms acute pancreatitis over uncomplicated hyperemesis?
probes.a: Serum lipase elevated more than three times the upper limit of normal.

rubric.text: Differentiates molar pregnancy and multiple gestation using ultrasonography
Distinguishes gastroenteritis, appendicitis, and pyelonephritis by pain, fever, and urinalysis
Excludes diabetic ketoacidosis, pancreatitis, and overt hyperthyroidism with targeted tests

skill.ix.hyperemesi.workup.title: Diagnostic and baseline workup in hyperemesis gravidarum
skill.ix.hyperemesi.workup.oneLine: Targeted laboratory and ultrasonographic investigations to grade severity, guide rehydration, and exclude mimics
skill.ix.hyperemesi.workup.why: Investigations in hyperemesis serve two mandatory functions: assessing dehydration, electrolyte depletion, and organ stress, and excluding alternative diagnoses. Routine urine dipstick, renal and liver panels, and pelvic ultrasound are essential for safe resuscitation and rule out hydatidiform mole and twins.

teach.heading: Urinalysis and Renal Function Assessment
teach.body:
Urinalysis by dipstick is the initial point-of-care test. It quantifies ketonuria (grades 1+ to 4+), indicating carbohydrate starvation, and measures specific gravity to confirm dehydration. Negative nitrites and leucocytes rule out urinary tract infection.

Renal function testing includes serum urea, creatinine, and electrolytes. Prerenal azotaemia with an elevated urea-to-creatinine ratio reflects hypovolaemia, while high haematocrit on blood count confirms hemoconcentration.

teach.heading: Electrolyte, Acid-Base, and Hepatic Profiling
teach.body:
Serum electrolytes typically demonstrate hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, and hypochloraemia. Venous or arterial blood gas testing reveals hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis from stomach acid loss, or metabolic acidosis if starvation ketosis predominates.

Liver transaminases (AST and ALT) are mildly elevated (two- to three-fold) in up to fifty percent of severe cases. Bilirubin remains normal or only slightly raised; marked jaundice demands evaluation for viral hepatitis or acute liver injury.

teach.heading: Pelvic Ultrasonography and Endocrine Testing
teach.body:
Pelvic ultrasound is non-negotiable. It confirms a live intrauterine fetus, establishes accurate gestational age, and excludes twin pregnancy and molar disease (gestational trophoblastic disease).

Thyroid function testing often reveals suppressed TSH and elevated free thyroxine (FT4). This transient gestational thyrotoxicosis is driven by hCG stimulating the TSH receptor, resolves spontaneously by twenty weeks, and requires no antithyroid medication.

probes.q: What initial point-of-care urine test confirms starvation ketosis and dehydration?
probes.a: Urine dipstick demonstrating ketonuria and high specific gravity.

probes.q: How should transient biochemical hyperthyroidism with low TSH and high FT4 be managed in hyperemesis?
probes.a: With supportive observation; it is self-limiting and does not require antithyroid drug therapy.

probes.q: What pattern of liver enzyme elevation is commonly seen in severe hyperemesis, and when does it resolve?
probes.a: Mild transaminitis with AST and ALT elevated two to three times normal, resolving with rehydration.

rubric.text: Interprets ketonuria, elevated specific gravity, and prerenal azotaemia
Evaluates hypokalaemic hypochloraemic alkalosis and mild transaminase elevation
Uses ultrasound to exclude molar pregnancy and recognises self-limiting gestational thyrotoxicosis

skill.hyperemesi.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and severity stratification in hyperemesis gravidarum
skill.hyperemesi.diagnosis.oneLine: Establishing the diagnosis by exclusion, stratifying clinical severity, and detecting organ complications
skill.hyperemesi.diagnosis.why: Hyperemesis gravidarum is diagnosed when severe early pregnancy nausea and vomiting occurs with weight loss greater than 5 percent, ketonuria, and electrolyte derangements in the absence of an alternative medical condition. Accurate severity stratification guides the site of care between outpatient ambulatory rehydration and emergency inpatient admission.

teach.heading: Formal Diagnostic Criteria and Exclusionary Seam
teach.body:
Hyperemesis gravidarum remains a clinical diagnosis reached after methodically excluding other causes of vomiting. The formal criteria require symptoms starting in early pregnancy, intractable vomiting, and inability to maintain oral hydration.

Objective confirmation rests on documented weight loss exceeding five percent of measured pre-pregnancy weight, ketonuria with starvation (typically 2+ or more in severe disease), and associated electrolyte abnormalities, without fever or localized peritoneal signs.

Mild and moderate grades in the table below describe the broader nausea and vomiting spectrum that does not meet these full criteria; only the severe grade corresponds to hyperemesis gravidarum.

teach.heading: Screening for Red Flags and High-Risk Complications
teach.body:
Inpatient admission is mandatory for women unable to maintain oral hydration, those with severe ketonuria, or those exhibiting significant weight loss. Immediate escalation to multidisciplinary care is triggered by danger signs.

These red flags include haemodynamic instability, severe refractory hypokalaemia under 3.0 mmol/L, haematemesis, or any neurological abnormality such as ataxia, nystagmus, or acute confusion signalling impending Wernicke encephalopathy.

probes.q: What defines hyperemesis gravidarum after excluding secondary medical causes?
probes.a: Intractable vomiting in early pregnancy with weight loss exceeding five percent, ketonuria, and electrolyte imbalance.

probes.q: Which clinical setting is appropriate for a patient with a moderate PUQE score and 3 percent weight loss?
probes.a: An ambulatory daycare rehydration unit with intravenous fluids and antiemetics.

probes.q: Name two clinical red flags in hyperemesis that mandate immediate inpatient admission and escalation.
probes.a: Neurological signs of Wernicke encephalopathy and haematemesis or severe hypokalaemia.

rubric.text: Applies diagnostic criteria of intractable vomiting, weight loss over 5 percent, and ketonuria
Stratifies clinical severity to guide outpatient, daycare, or inpatient admission
Identifies neurological signs, haematemesis, and severe electrolyte derangement

skill.tx.hyperemesi.title: Managing hyperemesis gravidarum
skill.tx.hyperemesi.oneLine: Intravenous crystalloid rehydration, mandatory thiamine before dextrose, stepwise antiemetic therapy, and thromboprophylaxis
skill.tx.hyperemesi.why: Effective therapy requires rapid correction of hypovolaemia and electrolytes, cessation of emesis through rational stepwise antiemetic regimens, and strict prevention of thiamine deficiency. Withholding glucose until thiamine is replenished is the single most critical safety rule in hyperemesis care, protecting against fatal Wernicke encephalopathy.
skill.tx.hyperemesi.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of drug class and principle. Specific agents, doses, routes and regimens must be taken from your current national or institutional guideline at the time of prescribing. CliniX does not prescribe.

teach.heading: Intravenous Fluid Rehydration and Electrolyte Replacement
teach.body:
Initial resuscitation requires isotonic crystalloids. Normal saline (0.9 percent sodium chloride) or Hartmann solution is the fluid of choice, restoring extracellular volume and correcting hypochloraemia.

Potassium chloride is added to maintenance fluids only once urine output is verified, at the concentration and rate in the local protocol under senior supervision, with continuous ECG monitoring and serial potassium checks.



Avoid glucose-containing fluids initially because infusing dextrose without thiamine precipitates acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

teach.heading: Mandatory Thiamine Repletion and Neurological Safety
teach.body:
Thiamine (vitamin B1) stores are rapidly depleted by prolonged starvation and persistent emesis. Administer parenteral thiamine at the prophylactic dose in the local protocol to every admitted patient before or alongside intravenous fluids. If nystagmus, ataxia, or confusion suggests Wernicke encephalopathy, escalate urgently to the high-dose intravenous thiamine regimen under senior supervision.

Dextrose administration accelerates carbohydrate oxidation, rapidly consuming remaining thiamine pyrophosphate cofactors. Co-administer pyridoxine and ensure serum magnesium is corrected, as hypomagnesaemia prevents thiamine utilisation.

rows: Mild to moderate emesis; safe throughout early pregnancy
Persistent vomiting; watch for dystonia with metoclopramide
Severe refractory illness beyond 10 weeks gestation

teach.heading: Thromboprophylaxis, Nutrition, and Discharge Criteria
teach.body:
Severe dehydration combined with pregnancy hypercoagulability dramatically escalates venous thromboembolism risk. Provide graduated compression stockings and prophylactic low molecular weight heparin during inpatient hospitalisation.

Discontinue oral iron supplements until vomiting completely resolves. Discharge requires tolerance of oral fluids, cleared ketonuria, and stable electrolytes. Counsel that recurrence is common and that severe hyperemesis recurs in about 1 in 5 future gestations, so early review is advised in the next pregnancy.

probes.q: What is the primary intravenous crystalloid recommended for initial rehydration in hyperemesis?
probes.a: Normal saline (0.9 percent sodium chloride) or Hartmann solution.

probes.q: Why must intravenous thiamine always be administered before any glucose or dextrose infusion?
probes.a: To prevent precipitating acute Wernicke encephalopathy caused by rapid thiamine consumption.

probes.q: Which antiemetic drug class is recommended as first-line therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?
probes.a: H1 antihistamines such as doxylamine with pyridoxine or promethazine.

rubric.text: Selects isotonic saline or Hartmann solution and supplements potassium per local protocol under senior supervision with ECG monitoring after confirming urine flow
Enforces mandatory thiamine administration before dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Navigates stepwise antiemetics from antihistamines to dopamine antagonists, 5-HT3 blockers, and steroids

cases.title: A 24-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks gestation with intractable vomiting and weight loss

patient.name: Meera Sharma
patient.residence: Urban, lives in Pune with her husband and mother-in-law

cases.opening: Doctor, please help me. For the past week I have been vomiting ten to fifteen times every day, and since yesterday I cannot even keep down a single sip of water.
cases.fallback: I feel very weak and dizzy, doctor. Can you please repeat what you are asking about?

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Lying in bed, visibly exhausted and pale. Eyes appear sunken with dry mucous membranes, dry cracked lips, furred tongue, and poor skin turgor with delayed recoil. A distinct sweetish, acetone odour is noted on the breath.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 116 beats per minute, regular, low volume. Blood pressure 94/58 mmHg supine, falling to 80/50 mmHg upon sitting with postural dizziness. Respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. Temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air.

skill.gen.edema.finding: No pedal oedema, no facial puffiness, no sacral oedema. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill time prolonged at 3 seconds, indicating peripheral vasoconstriction from volume depletion.

skill.gen.cyanosis.finding: No central or peripheral cyanosis. Tongue and conjunctivae are dry and pale.

skill.exam.obg.preg_prep_inspect.finding: Abdomen is scaphoid, flat, and relaxed. No visible distension, no peristalsis, and no surgical scars or striae.

skill.exam.obg.fundal_height.finding: Uterus is not palpable per abdomen above the symphysis pubis, consistent with early gestational age of 9 weeks. Mild non-specific epigastric tenderness on deep palpation from frequent retching; no guarding, no rigidity, and normal bowel sounds.

urine_dipstick.label: Urine dipstick
urine_dipstick.result: Ketones 3+ (strongly positive), specific gravity 1.032, protein negative, glucose negative, nitrites negative, leucocyte esterase negative.
urine_dipstick.note: Severe ketonuria and high specific gravity confirm starvation ketosis and profound volume depletion; negative nitrites and leucocytes exclude urinary tract infection.

serum_electrolytes.label: Serum electrolytes
serum_electrolytes.result: Sodium 131 mmol/L (mild hyponatraemia), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (hypokalaemia), chloride 92 mmol/L (hypochloraemia), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (metabolic alkalosis).
serum_electrolytes.note: Loss of hydrochloric acid from gastric emesis produces hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis requiring potassium-supplemented saline rehydration per the local protocol once urine output is verified, with ECG monitoring and serial potassium checks under senior supervision.

renal_function.label: Renal function tests
renal_function.result: Blood urea 44 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, serum uric acid 6.8 mg/dL.
renal_function.note: Elevated urea and creatinine indicate prerenal acute kidney injury secondary to dehydration; uric acid is elevated due to ketosis and hemoconcentration.

liver_function.label: Liver function tests
liver_function.result: Total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, AST (SGOT) 78 U/L (mildly elevated), ALT (SGPT) 86 U/L (mildly elevated), alkaline phosphatase 95 U/L, serum albumin 4.2 g/dL.
liver_function.note: Mild transaminitis (2 to 3 times upper limit of normal) occurs in up to fifty percent of severe hyperemesis and resolves with hydration; normal bilirubin argues against primary hepatobiliary disease.

complete_blood_count.label: Complete blood count
complete_blood_count.result: Haemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, haematocrit 43 percent (hemoconcentration), total leucocyte count 8,600 /cu mm, platelet count 260,000 /cu mm.
complete_blood_count.note: High haematocrit reflects plasma volume contraction and dehydration.

pelvic_ultrasound.label: Pelvic ultrasound
pelvic_ultrasound.result: Single live intrauterine pregnancy, crown-rump length corresponding to 9 weeks 1 day, regular fetal cardiac activity at 168 beats per minute. Normal gestational sac, no subchorionic haemorrhage. Bilateral ovaries normal without theca lutein cysts. No evidence of vesicular molar changes or multiple gestation.
pelvic_ultrasound.note: Confirms viable singleton pregnancy and rules out gestational trophoblastic disease (hydatidiform mole) and twin pregnancy.

thyroid_function.label: Thyroid function tests
thyroid_function.result: Serum TSH 0.15 mIU/L (suppressed), free T4 22.8 pmol/L (mildly elevated), thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies negative, TSH receptor antibodies negative.
thyroid_function.note: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis caused by high circulating hCG cross-reacting with the TSH receptor; self-limiting and does not require antithyroid drug therapy.

serum_lipase_amylase.label: Serum amylase and lipase
serum_lipase_amylase.result: Serum amylase 92 U/L (normal), serum lipase 42 U/L (normal).
serum_lipase_amylase.note: Normal pancreatic enzymes rule out acute pancreatitis as a secondary cause of intractable vomiting.

blood_glucose.label: Random blood glucose
blood_glucose.note: Euglycaemia with ketonuria confirms starvation ketosis and rules out diabetic ketoacidosis.

differentialModel.answer: Hyperemesis gravidarum, with secondary dehydration, hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, and starvation ketonuria. Key differentials to exclude are gestational trophoblastic disease (molar pregnancy), multiple pregnancy, acute gastroenteritis, acute pyelonephritis, peptic ulcer disease, acute pancreatitis, diabetic ketoacidosis, and hyperthyroidism.

diagnosis.answer: Hyperemesis gravidarum in a 9-week primigravida, complicated by severe dehydration, starvation ketosis, hypokalaemia, and prerenal azotaemia, with tiny brown specks in vomitus suggesting minor mucosal bleeding (?Mallory-Weiss tear) for evaluation.

managementModel.answer: Hospital admission, intravenous rehydration with normal saline or Hartmann solution, potassium chloride replacement per the local protocol with ECG monitoring once urine output is verified, parenteral thiamine before any dextrose infusion to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy with urgent escalation to the high-dose regimen if neurological signs appear, stepwise antiemetic therapy with promethazine or metoclopramide, assessment of the brown specks as possible minor haematemesis from retching with senior review and escalation for fresh blood, melaena, or instability, thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin, withholding oral iron tablets, serial monitoring of fluid balance, weight, urinary ketones and electrolytes, and gradual reintroduction of light oral sips once vomiting subsides.

teachingPoints: Hyperemesis gravidarum is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion defined by severe intractable early pregnancy nausea and vomiting leading to dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, ketonuria, and weight loss greater than 5 percent of pre-pregnancy weight.
Parenteral thiamine must ALWAYS be administered before or concurrently with any glucose or dextrose infusion to prevent precipitating acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

The primary rehydration fluid is normal saline (0.9 percent sodium chloride) or Hartmann solution, with potassium chloride added only once urine output is verified, at the concentration and rate in the local protocol under senior supervision with ECG monitoring, correcting the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Pelvic ultrasound is mandatory in every patient with suspected hyperemesis to confirm viability and actively exclude multiple pregnancy and gestational trophoblastic disease (molar pregnancy).

Antiemetic pharmacotherapy follows a stepwise escalation from first-line antihistamines or phenothiazines to dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide) or ondansetron, reserving corticosteroids for severe refractory cases after 10 weeks gestation.

Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH and elevated free T4 is driven by hCG cross-reactivity at the TSH receptor, resolves spontaneously by 18 to 20 weeks, and does not require antithyroid medications.

Severe dehydration in pregnancy significantly elevates venous thromboembolism risk, warranting thromboprophylaxis with graduated compression stockings and low molecular weight heparin during inpatient admission.
